title: Have You Ever Seen the Rain?
trivia: John Fogerty wrote it as the band was coming apart, with his brother Tom about to quit. The sunny-day rain image is often read as a metaphor for trouble arriving when things look fine.

track.title: Have You Ever Seen the Rain?

notes: Album Dec 1970, single Jan 1971.

title: Your Song
trivia: Bernie Taupin scribbled the lyrics at a breakfast table, and Elton John reportedly set them to music within minutes.
notes: Album Apr 1970; single followed in Oct 1970.

title: You Can Get It If You Really Want
trivia: Jimmy Cliff's original later opened the film The Harder They Come. Desmond Dekker's version over the same backing track charted higher in the UK.

track.title: You Can Get It If You Really Want
track.notes: Jimmy Cliff original, not Desmond Dekker.

notes: Original UK single on Trojan, July 1970 (no album at the time).

title: In the Summertime
trivia: The jug-band stomp spent seven weeks at number one in the UK in the summer of 1970.

title: Signed, Sealed, Delivered (I'm Yours)
trivia: Stevie Wonder co-wrote it with his mother Lula Mae Hardaway and others, and co-produced it, an early sign of his growing independence at Motown.

title: Let It Be
trivia: Paul McCartney has said the title came to him from his late mother Mary, who appeared to him in a dream.

track.title: Let It Be
track.notes: Single or album version, both fine.

notes: Single Mar 1970 (3:50); the album version (May 1970) has a different guitar solo and runs longer.

title: Lola
trivia: The BBC would not play a lyric naming Coca-Cola, so Ray Davies flew back from a US tour to re-record it with cherry cola.

track.title: Lola
track.album: Lola Versus Powerman and the Moneygoround, Part One

title: Life on Mars?
trivia: Bowie wrote it as a playful answer to a song whose English lyrics he had been asked to write but which were turned down. It was only released as a single in 1973.
notes: Album Dec 1971 (the single came in 1973).

title: American Pie
trivia: The song is about the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and the Big Bopper. The full 8:36 version was split over both sides of the single.
notes: Album Oct 1971; the single (Nov 1971) was split in two parts. Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Canada edition list.

title: Non, non, rien n'a changé
trivia: Les Poppys were a French group of young singers. This French-language single also became a hit in the Netherlands.
notes: Hitster NL lists 1971. Not widely documented; conf medium. French children's vocal group, original French-language single.

title: Maggie May
trivia: Radio DJs flipped the single over, making what was meant as the B-side of Reason to Believe the real hit. Ray Jackson of Lindisfarne played the mandolin part.
notes: Album May 1971; single Jul 1971. Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Canada edition list.

title: You're So Vain
trivia: Mick Jagger sings uncredited backing vocals. Carly Simon has famously kept the target of the lyrics a mystery for decades.

title: Crazy Horses
trivia: The Osmonds' heavy-sounding single is really an environmental protest, with crazy horses standing in for polluting cars.
notes: Single Jul 1972; album Nov 1972 (album version runs longer).

title: Piano Man
trivia: Billy Joel drew on his time as a lounge pianist in Los Angeles, where he played under a false name. The 5:38 album version is the one most people know.
notes: Album and single both Nov 1973 (single edit is shorter).

title: Jolene
trivia: Dolly Parton has said she wrote this and I Will Always Love You on the same day. The title character was inspired by a red-haired bank clerk who flirted with her husband.
notes: Single Oct 1973; album Feb 1974.

title: Waterloo
trivia: ABBA won the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest with it in Brighton, which kick-started their international career.

title: You're the First, the Last, My Everything
trivia: Barry White opens with a spoken passage over swirling strings. In 1975 it gave him a UK number one.

track.title: You're the First, the Last, My Everything

notes: Album Aug 1974; single Nov 1974.

title: I Can Help
trivia: Billy Swan, a former bass player for Kris Kristofferson, scored a US number one with this laid-back tune and its homemade-sounding organ.

title: No Woman, No Cry
trivia: The song credits Vincent Ford, a friend who ran a soup kitchen in Trenchtown, so that he could collect royalties.

track.title: No Woman, No Cry
track.notes: Studio version from Natty Dread (1974), not the 1975 live version.

notes: Studio version is on Natty Dread (1974). The version most people know (on Legend) is the live Lyceum recording from July 1975, released as a single in Sept 1975. Hitster lists 1974.

title: Sweet Home Alabama
trivia: The band wrote it in part as an answer to Neil Young's songs about the American South. Its opening riff is among the best known in rock.

title: December, 1963 (Oh, What a Night)
trivia: Early drafts were about the end of Prohibition in 1933, before the lyric was reworked into a story about a lost night in 1963. Drummer Gerry Polci sings the lead.

title: Bohemian Rhapsody
trivia: Freddie Mercury's six-minute mini-opera has no chorus. The record company feared it was too long for radio, but a DJ who got hold of an advance copy played it repeatedly.
notes: Single Oct 1975; album Nov 1975. Not seen on any consulted Hitster edition list (NL, DE, FR, CA, Nordics); added for recognisability and decade balance.

title: I Love Rock 'n' Roll
trivia: Written by Alan Merrill and Jake Hooker of the Arrows. Joan Jett saw the band perform it on TV in Britain and later turned it into her own hit.

track.title: I Love Rock 'n' Roll
track.notes: The Arrows original, not Joan Jett.

notes: Original UK single by The Arrows (Rak, 1975), not the later Joan Jett cover; Hitster NL lists this version. Release date within 1975 not pinned down.

title: The Hustle
trivia: Van McCoy named the track after a New York dance. Its flute hook helped it top the US pop and R&B charts.
notes: Credited on release to Van McCoy and the Soul City Symphony.

title: Dancing Queen
trivia: It was first performed on a Swedish TV gala held on the eve of the king's wedding. It is ABBA's only US number one.
notes: Single Aug 1976; album Oct 1976. Not seen on any consulted Hitster edition list (NL, DE, FR, CA, Nordics); added for recognisability and decade balance.

title: Daddy Cool
trivia: The group was put together by producer Frank Farian, who also sang the deep male vocals on their records, while the dancer on stage mimed along.

title: More Than a Feeling
trivia: Tom Scholz, an MIT-trained engineer, recorded most of the band's debut in his home basement studio.
notes: Album Aug 1976; single Sept 1976.

title: Let's Stick Together
trivia: Bryan Ferry gave an R&B tune a stylish makeover and took it into the UK top five. It was first recorded by Wilbert Harrison.
notes: Cover of Wilbert Harrison's Let's Stick Together (1962). Hitster NL lists Ferry's version; kept for recognisability. Album: Let's Stick Together (Sept 1976).

title: If You Leave Me Now
trivia: Peter Cetera wrote and sang it, and it gave Chicago their first number one in both the US and the UK.

title: Hotel California
trivia: Don Felder came up with the music on a demo, and the lyrics are widely read as a comment on the excesses of Californian life. The long twin-guitar outro is famous.
notes: Album Dec 1976; single Feb 1977. Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Canada edition list.

title: When I Need You
trivia: The song was written by Albert Hammond and Carole Bayer Sager. Hammond released it first, but Leo Sayer's version went to number one in both the UK and the US.

track.title: When I Need You
track.notes: Leo Sayer version, not Albert Hammond.

notes: Album Endless Flight came out 29 Oct 1976; the single followed in Feb 1977 (the hit year). Card uses 1976 per album-first rule; Hitster NL lists 1977. Cover of Albert Hammond's 1976 version. Hitster NL list shows 1977; card uses 1976.

title: Disco Inferno
trivia: The track is a Philadelphia dance-floor classic that urges everyone to burn. It was added to a hit film soundtrack the following year.
notes: Original album Disco Inferno (1976). Single edit is shorter; the album version is preferred.

title: Don't Leave Me This Way
trivia: Thelma Houston's disco take on a song first recorded by Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes won a Grammy.

track.title: Don't Leave Me This Way
track.notes: Thelma Houston version, not Harold Melvin.

notes: Cover of Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes (1975), but Houston's is the famous recording. An album version is longer.

title: Stayin' Alive
trivia: The Bee Gees wrote it for the film Saturday Night Fever. Its beat of about 103 per minute is often cited as a rhythm for teaching CPR.
notes: Album Nov 1977; single Dec 1977. Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Canada edition list.

title: Easy
trivia: Lionel Richie wrote this ballad about leaving a relationship, and it helped the Commodores move from funk towards softer songs.

title: Blue Bayou
trivia: Ronstadt's cover of a Roy Orbison song reached the US top three. Orbison co-wrote and first recorded it in 1963.

track.title: Blue Bayou
track.notes: Linda Ronstadt version, not Roy Orbison.

notes: Cover of Roy Orbison (1963), but Ronstadt's is the version most people know.

title: Paradise by the Dashboard Light
trivia: The spoken baseball commentary in the middle is delivered by Phil Rizzuto, a former New York Yankees shortstop and broadcaster.
notes: Album Oct 1977; the edited single followed in early 1978. Album version preferred. Hitster NL lists 1978. Hitster NL list shows 1978; card uses 1977.

title: Knock on Wood
trivia: Amii Stewart's disco remake of the 1966 soul hit by Eddie Floyd, co-written with Steve Cropper, reached number one in the US.

track.title: Knock on Wood
track.notes: Amii Stewart disco version, not Eddie Floyd.

notes: Single released 1978 (Discogs; UK 7-inch), album Feb 1979. Hitster NL lists 1979. Cover of Eddie Floyd (1966). Hitster NL list shows 1979; card uses 1978.

title: Heart of Glass
trivia: Blondie began it as a slower reggae-tinged demo and reworked it with a drum machine. Some punk fans disliked the move towards disco.
notes: Album Sept 1978; single Jan 1979. Album version preferred (the single edit is shorter). Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Canada edition list.

title: Le Freak
trivia: Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards wrote it after being turned away from Studio 54 on New Year's Eve. The famous shout in the chorus started out as a much ruder phrase.
notes: Single Aug 1978; album Oct 1978. Album version is longer than the single edit.

title: September
trivia: Co-writer Allee Willis disliked the nonsense ba-de-ya line, but bandleader Maurice White insisted it stay.

track.title: September
track.album: The Best of Earth, Wind & Fire, Vol. 1

notes: First released on the compilation The Best of Earth, Wind & Fire Vol. 1 (Nov 1978) and as a single the same month. Not seen on any consulted Hitster edition list (NL, DE, FR, CA, Nordics); added for recognisability and decade balance.

title: I Will Survive
trivia: It started life as the B-side of another single, until DJs started playing the flip side.
notes: Single Oct 1978; album Love Tracks Nov 1978. The 7-inch edit is about 3:18; the album version is longer. Not on the Hitster NL list; seen on the Hitster Canada edition list.

title: Born to Be Alive
trivia: Patrick Hernandez's French disco smash made him a star overseas. A young Madonna later worked as one of his backing dancers.
notes: Single released 1978 in France; international hit 1979; album 1979.

title: You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real)
trivia: Sylvester's soaring falsetto, backed by the group Two Tons o' Fun, made this the signature song of the self-styled Queen of Disco.
notes: 7-inch edit is about 3:30; longer 12-inch/album versions exist.

title: Escape (The Piña Colada Song)
trivia: The lyric ends with a twist: a man answers a personals ad for a fellow Piña Colada fan, only to find his own partner placed it.
notes: Album Sept 1979; single Dec 1979. Song was originally titled Escape.

title: We Are Family
trivia: Written and produced by Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards for the Sledge sisters. It became the adopted anthem of the Pittsburgh Pirates in 1979.
notes: Single Apr 1979; the album version runs longer.
